quizzes.title: MA1 Quiz #1
quizzes.blurb: History, Universal Precautions, communication, SOAP, SUDS and blood pressure.
quizzes.sgNote: 1–32 follow the study guide in order; 33 is its review line.

topics.2: Agent of disease most likely encountered
topics.3: What Universal Precautions are / who they protect
topics.20: Swedish massage comes to the U.S.

questions.q: A pathogen is defined as:
questions.a: A biological agent capable of causing disease
w: An inanimate object that carries disease
The reproductive unit of a fungus
A chemical used to disinfect surfaces
questions.e: Pathogen = biological agent capable of causing disease.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a type of pathogen listed in the lecture?
questions.e: Pathogens: bacteria, fungi, viruses, protozoa, animal parasites. A fomite is an object that carries them.

questions.q: Bacteria, fungi, viruses and animal parasites are all examples of:
questions.e: These are the agents that cause disease (pathogens).

questions.q: A massage table, a shared towel, or a door handle that carries disease is called a:
questions.e: Fomite = inanimate object that transmits disease.

questions.q: Which term means 'a biological agent capable of causing disease'?
questions.e: Pathogen is the lecture's definition word.

questions.q: Which agent of disease is a massage therapist MOST likely to be exposed to?
questions.e: Slide callout: fungi are the most common pathogen massage therapists will be exposed to.

questions.q: The most common pathogen massage therapists will be exposed to is:
questions.e: Fungi, especially tinea (ringworm).

questions.q: Fungi thrive in which environment?
questions.e: Fungal agents (molds and yeast) thrive in warm, moist environments.

questions.q: Fungal infections are generally transmitted by:
questions.e: Generally by a fomite; can also spread via touch.

questions.q: Tinea pedis is commonly known as:
questions.e: Pedis = foot.

questions.q: Tinea capitis (ringworm of the head) is most common in:
questions.e: Capitis is most common in children; cruris (jock itch) in men and adolescent boys.

questions.q: Tinea unguium affects the:
questions.e: Unguium = nails.

questions.q: Fungal infections are described as:
questions.a: Superficial, tenacious and difficult to eradicate
w: Deep, mild and easy to cure
questions.e: Superficial, tenacious, hard to eradicate, very contagious, 2-3 week incubation.

questions.q: Universal Precautions protect:
questions.a: Both the client and the therapist
questions.e: They protect client AND therapist from disease transmission.

questions.q: If standards and guidelines are NOT followed, who is at risk of disease or injury?
questions.a: Both the client and the therapist
questions.e: Slide 3 highlights 'DO NOT FOLLOW': both client and therapist are at risk.

questions.q: Universal Precautions were established by:
questions.a: OSHA and the CDC in the early 1990s
questions.e: OSHA & CDC, early 1990s.

questions.q: The core assumption behind Universal Precautions is:
questions.a: Every individual has a potentially infectious condition
w: Only visibly ill clients are infectious
Clients will disclose all infections on the intake form
questions.e: Assume EVERY individual is potentially infectious.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the main principles of Universal Precautions for massage therapists?
questions.e: Main principles: sanitation, hygiene, glove use, handwashing, careful handling of blood and body fluids.

questions.q: Therapists working in which setting have a greater risk of exposure to pathogens?
questions.e: Medical settings carry greater exposure risk.

questions.q: Which body fluid is listed as a concern under Universal Precautions?
questions.e: Listed: blood, saliva, mucus, semen, vaginal secretions, cerebrospinal, synovial, pleural, peritoneal, pericardial fluids.

questions.q: A massage therapist should wear gloves when:
questions.a: The therapist or client has a break in the skin
w: Using a cream instead of oil
questions.e: Broken skin on either person calls for gloves (finger cot if only one fingertip).

questions.q: If only the tip of one finger has a cut, the therapist can use a:
w: Full pair of latex gloves only
questions.e: Finger cot covers a single fingertip.

questions.q: Gloves are recommended for hygiene reasons during:
questions.e: TMJ work is the slide's hygiene example; the UP handout also lists examining the mouth.

questions.q: Which situation calls for gloves?
questions.a: Removing linens and trash that may be contaminated with body fluids
questions.e: Handling blood or body fluids includes possibly contaminated linens and trash.

questions.q: If the client does not want you to use gloves when they are needed, you:
questions.a: Have the right to refuse the massage
w: Use gloves on one hand only
questions.e: You may refuse to do the massage.

questions.q: Which is TRUE about glove use?
questions.a: Wash hands before and after using gloves
w: Gloves reduce friction on hairy skin
questions.e: Wash before and after; gloves reduce palpation and add friction, especially over thick hair.

questions.q: If a glove tears during a massage, you should:
questions.a: Wash your hands and put on a new glove
questions.e: Damaged glove: wash hands, new glove.

questions.q: The difference between disinfection and sterilization is:
questions.a: Sterilization destroys all pathogens; disinfection may not remove spores
w: Disinfection destroys spores; sterilization does not
Sterilization uses only soap and water
questions.e: Disinfection removes pathogens from a surface but does not always remove spores.

questions.q: Which process does NOT always remove spores?
questions.e: Disinfection does not always remove spores (the reproductive unit).

questions.q: Disinfection removes pathogens from a surface using:
questions.e: Chemical or mechanical agent; heat/steam methods are sterilization.

questions.q: Which is a method of STERILIZATION?
questions.e: Sterilization: heat, water, chemicals or gases, e.g. autoclave or baking.

questions.q: Dry-heat sterilization in the lecture is baking at:
questions.e: Bake at 350°F for 1 hour.

questions.q: A spore is:
questions.a: The reproductive unit of a microorganism
questions.e: Spore = reproductive unit; may survive disinfection.

questions.q: The UP handout says areas soiled with blood should be cleaned with disinfectant and rinsed with:
questions.a: 1 part chlorine bleach to 10 parts water
questions.e: Rinse with a 1:10 bleach solution.

questions.q: 'The application of measures to promote a healthful, disease-free environment' defines:
questions.e: Sanitation is the umbrella term.

questions.q: The primary source of microorganism cross-contamination is:
questions.e: Contact with human hands.

questions.q: The best way to control cross-contamination is:
questions.e: Best control = HAND WASHING.

questions.q: When should you wash your hands?
w: Only before the first massage of the day
questions.e: Slide callout: WASH HANDS BEFORE & AFTER EACH MASSAGE.

questions.q: According to the UP handout, you should wash your hands:
w: Only at the end of the day
questions.e: Also before/after eating, after the restroom, after any body-fluid contact.

questions.q: The most important aspect of handwashing is:
questions.e: Friction emulsifies skin oil and removes microorganisms and dirt.

questions.q: Friction during handwashing is essential because it:
questions.a: Emulsifies the oil on the skin and removes microorganisms and dirt
questions.e: Friction emulsifies skin oil and lifts microbes and dirt.

questions.q: The recommended time to rub soap up the forearms is:
questions.e: 15-30 seconds, 2 minutes if needed.

questions.q: When rinsing, water should run:
questions.a: From the fingers to the elbows
w: From the elbows to the fingers
questions.e: Fingers to elbows keeps the hands the cleanest area.

questions.q: At the start of handwashing, the hands should be:
questions.e: Start with hands lower than the elbows.

questions.q: Which soap is preferred?
questions.e: Liquid soap is preferred over bar soap.

questions.q: After drying your hands, the paper towel should be used to:
questions.a: Turn off the water and open door handles, then be discarded
w: Be saved for the next wash
questions.e: Use the same towel for the faucet and door handles until you reach the massage area.

questions.q: Hygiene is best defined as:
questions.a: The science and practice of preserving health and preventing disease through cleanliness
w: The removal of pathogens from a surface
A biological agent capable of causing disease
questions.e: Hygiene = practices that preserve health. (Not on slides; standard definition.)

questions.q: Which is a personal hygiene guideline from the lecture?
questions.e: Short clean nails, no jewelry, no perfume, no gum.

questions.q: Which should a massage therapist AVOID?
questions.e: Avoid perfumes and scented cosmetics.

questions.q: Which food does the lecture say to avoid before working with clients?
questions.e: Avoid offensive foods: garlic, onions, etc.

questions.q: Personal hygiene for therapists includes:
questions.e: No jewelry, no gum, no smoking around clients or before a massage.

questions.q: Massage is defined as:
questions.a: Systematic and scientific manipulation of the soft tissues of the body for the purpose of obtaining or maintaining health
w: Random rubbing of the skin for relaxation only
Manipulation of the bones to correct alignment
questions.e: The highlighted definition on slide 4.

questions.q: According to the definition, massage manipulates the:
questions.e: Soft tissues.

questions.q: The purpose of massage in the definition is:
questions.e: For the purpose of obtaining or maintaining health.

questions.q: About how many types of massage and bodywork are used in the world today?
questions.e: Over 75 types.

questions.q: Which two words describe how massage manipulates tissue, per the definition?
questions.e: Systematic and scientific manipulation.

questions.q: Which is a general benefit of massage?
questions.a: Increases the oxygen capacity of blood
questions.e: Benefits: reduce stress, enhance circulation, decrease pain, promote sleep, reduce swelling, enhance relaxation, increase blood oxygen capacity.

questions.q: Which is NOT listed as a benefit of massage?
questions.e: Sterilizing is not a massage effect.

questions.q: Massage affects circulation by:
questions.e: Enhance blood circulation.

questions.q: Which set lists only benefits of massage?
questions.a: Decrease pain, promote sleep, enhance relaxation
w: Decrease pain, increase swelling, raise stress
Promote sleep, spread infection, decrease circulation
Reduce stress, cure disease, increase swelling
questions.e: All three are on the benefits slide.

questions.q: Massage therapy is described as one of the healthcare field's:
questions.a: Safest and least obtrusive yet effective modalities
questions.e: Safest, least obtrusive, yet effective.

questions.q: The first culture to DOCUMENT the use of massage was:
questions.e: Documented use in China dates back to 3000 BC.

questions.q: Documented use of massage in China dates back to about:
questions.e: 3000 BC, about 5,000 years ago.

questions.q: Which culture was the first to train blind therapists?
questions.e: Starred in red on slide 10.

questions.q: Cave paintings from about 15,000 years ago:
w: Are the first written record of massage
questions.e: They imply massage; China has the first documentation.

questions.q: Acupuncture first appeared in Chinese medical writings around:
questions.e: 90 BC; the precursor of all other manual or energetic therapies.

questions.q: The Huang-ti nei-ching is:
questions.a: The classic scripture of Traditional Chinese Medicine
questions.e: Compiled under the mythical Yellow Emperor.

questions.q: Chinese therapies are called 'the grandparents of ALL techniques' because:
questions.a: They are the precursor of all other manual or energetic therapies
questions.e: Precursor of all others.

questions.q: Amma is:
questions.a: A Chinese technique of rubbing, pressing and manipulating specific points
questions.e: Amma (Amna, Ammo) comes from the classic scripture of TCM.

questions.q: Amma originates from which culture?
questions.e: Chinese, from the classic scripture of TCM.

questions.q: Which technique involves rubbing, pressing and manipulating specific points?
questions.e: Amma.

questions.q: Amma comes from:
questions.a: The classic scripture of Traditional Chinese Medicine
questions.e: From the classic TCM scripture.

questions.q: Shiatsu means:
questions.e: Shiatsu = finger pressure.

questions.q: Shiatsu comes from which country?
questions.e: Japan, 6th century AD.

questions.q: In Shiatsu, a tsubo is:
questions.e: Tsubo = energy point.

questions.q: The goal of Shiatsu is to:
questions.a: Bring balance between mind and body
questions.e: Balance between mind and body.

questions.q: Shiatsu developed in the:
questions.e: Japan, 6th century AD.

questions.q: In India, massage is an aspect of:
questions.e: Ayurveda took shape in the 6th-7th centuries BC.

questions.q: The current symbol of medicine, a snake and staff, is credited to:
questions.e: His holy snake and staff remain the symbol of the medical profession.

questions.q: Aesculapius was a:
questions.e: Greek priest-physician, 7th century BC.

questions.q: Aesculapius combined exercise and massage to create:
questions.e: Exercise + massage = gymnastics.

questions.q: Aesculapius was later revered as the:
questions.e: Later revered as the god of medicine.

questions.q: The symbol of the medical profession is:
questions.a: A snake coiled around a staff
questions.e: Aesculapius' holy snake and staff.

questions.q: The 'Father of Western Medicine' is:
questions.e: Hippocrates (460-375 BC).

questions.q: Hippocrates' philosophy included:
questions.a: The healer should cause NO additional harm
w: Drugs are the first choice of treatment
Treat the disease, not the patient
questions.e: Emphasize the individual patient; do no additional harm.

questions.q: Hippocrates was a proponent of massage, particularly:
questions.e: Particularly friction.

questions.q: The code of ethics associated with Hippocrates is the:
questions.e: Hippocratic Oath.

questions.q: Hippocrates emphasized:
questions.e: Emphasized the individual patient.

questions.q: William Harvey's discovery that helped establish massage as therapeutic was:
questions.a: Blood circulates through the arteries and veins by the beat of the heart
questions.e: Circulation driven by the heartbeat enhanced acceptance of massage.

questions.q: William Harvey was from:
Who discovered that arteries and veins CONTAIN blood (not that it circulates)?
questions.e: Galen: contain. Harvey: circulate via the heartbeat.

questions.q: Harvey's discovery affected massage by:
questions.a: Enhancing the acceptance of massage as therapeutic
questions.e: It enhanced the acceptance of massage as therapeutic.

questions.q: The 'Father of Swedish Massage' is:
questions.e: Ling (1776-1839), also father of physical therapy.

questions.q: Pehr Henrik Ling's system of medical gymnastics is known as the:
questions.e: Ling System → Swedish Movement → Swedish Movement Cure → Swedish Massage.

questions.q: Besides Swedish massage, Ling is also considered the father of:
questions.e: Father of Swedish massage and physical therapy.

questions.q: Ling was a:
questions.e: Swedish physiologist and gymnastics instructor.

questions.q: Which order shows how Ling's work evolved?
questions.a: Ling System → Swedish Movement → Swedish Movement Cure → Swedish Massage
w: Swedish Massage → Ling System → Swedish Movement
Swedish Movement Cure → Ling System → Swedish Massage
questions.e: The slide's sequence.

questions.q: Swedish massage is described as:
questions.a: Massage strokes in tandem with movement
questions.e: Strokes in tandem with movement.

questions.q: In Swedish massage, an ACTIVE movement is performed by the:
questions.e: Active = client; passive = therapist; duplicated = both.

questions.q: In Swedish massage, a PASSIVE movement is performed by the:
questions.e: Passive = therapist.

questions.q: A DUPLICATED movement is performed by:
questions.e: Duplicated = both.

questions.q: How many primary movements does Swedish massage have?
questions.e: Active, passive, duplicated.

questions.q: Which is a stated effect of Swedish massage?
questions.e: Improves circulation, relieves tension, improves ROM, promotes relaxation.

questions.q: Who is credited with much of the terminology for Swedish massage strokes?
questions.e: Mezger introduced French terminology.

questions.q: The Swedish massage stroke terms originate from which language?
questions.e: Effleurage, petrissage, tapotement are French.

questions.q: Effleurage, petrissage and tapotement are examples of:
questions.a: French terms introduced by Johann Mezger
questions.e: Mezger's French terminology.

questions.q: Johann Mezger made massage a fundamental component of:
questions.e: Physical rehabilitation; also promoted massage to the medical profession.

questions.q: Who introduced Swedish massage (the Swedish Movement) to the United States?
questions.a: George Henry Taylor and Charles Fayette Taylor
questions.e: The Taylors; starred on the slide.

questions.q: Swedish massage was introduced to the United States in:
questions.e: 1856. The first American textbook followed in 1860.

questions.q: The first American textbook on Swedish massage was published in:
questions.e: 1860, by the Taylors.

questions.q: John Harvey Kellogg is known for:
questions.a: Popularizing massage with the general public
w: Introducing Swedish massage to the U.S. in 1856
questions.e: Kellogg popularized it (Good Health magazine); the Taylors introduced it.

questions.q: The 3 types of professional communication are:
questions.e: Verbal, non-verbal, written.

questions.q: Professional communication with a client starts:
questions.a: When they call for an appointment
w: When they lie on the table
questions.e: Starts when they call for an appointment.

questions.q: Written communication should be:
questions.a: Checked with the client at each visit and updated
w: Filled out once and never changed
Kept only by the front desk
questions.e: Starred in red on the slide: always check with the client at each visit and update.

questions.q: Which is an example of WRITTEN communication?
questions.e: Intake form, consent form, prescriptions, SOAP notes, correspondence, referral forms.

questions.q: 'Speak it back to them in your own words and have them confirm' describes:
questions.e: A verbal communication skill.

questions.q: 'Sit if they sit, stand if they stand' describes:
questions.e: A non-verbal communication consideration.

questions.q: Good verbal communication with clients uses:
questions.e: Open, safe, non-judgmental; open-ended questions; empathy.

questions.q: Informed consent is:
questions.a: The client's authorization for professional services
questions.e: Starred on the slide.

questions.q: Informed consent can be:
questions.a: Written or verbal, but written is recommended
w: Assumed if the client shows up
questions.e: Written or verbal; get it in writing.

questions.q: Massage therapists have 'direct access' to the public. This means:
questions.a: No prescription or referral is needed to receive massage
w: A doctor must approve each session
Clients may skip the intake form
questions.e: Direct access = no prescription/referral needed.

questions.q: Most insurance companies require what before paying for massage?
questions.e: Insurance usually wants a prescription or referral.

questions.q: Informed consent is gained during the:
questions.e: Part of the pre-massage interview, after explaining services and benefits/side effects.

questions.q: The 4 categories of client treatment records are:
questions.e: SOAP. In medical settings A = Assessment.

questions.q: In SOAP notes, 'S' records:
questions.a: What the client tells you, in their words
questions.e: Subjective = client's words.

questions.q: In SOAP notes, 'O' records:
questions.a: Your findings: what you see, feel, hear, smell, sense
questions.e: Objective = your findings.

questions.q: In SOAP notes, 'A' (Action) records:
questions.a: What you did during the session: strokes, techniques, ROM, stretching
questions.e: Action = what you did. (Medical: Assessment.)

questions.q: In SOAP notes, 'P' records:
questions.a: What you intend and recommend: rescheduling, home care
questions.e: Plan.

questions.q: A client says, 'My neck hurts when I turn left.' This goes under:
questions.e: Client's own words = Subjective.

questions.q: You notice the client's right shoulder is elevated. This goes under:
questions.e: Your observation = Objective.

questions.q: You recommend neck stretches and a follow-up in one week. This goes under:
questions.e: Recommendations and rescheduling = Plan.

questions.q: A symptom is:
questions.a: A subjective change the client feels and reports
w: An objective finding the therapist measures
questions.e: Symptom = subjective. Sign = objective. (Not on slides; standard definition.)

questions.q: Symptoms are recorded in which part of the SOAP note?
questions.e: Client-reported, so Subjective.

questions.q: Which is a SYMPTOM rather than a sign?
questions.e: Symptoms are felt and reported by the client.

questions.q: Something the therapist can observe or measure, like swelling, is called a:
questions.e: Sign = objective.

questions.q: A short-term goal focuses on:
questions.a: The immediate problem, such as decreasing pain in the current session
questions.e: Short-term = immediate problem, this session.

questions.q: A long-term goal focuses on:
w: Decreasing pain in the current session only
questions.e: Long-term = restore function; decrease frequency and intensity of symptoms.

questions.q: 'Decrease the frequency and intensity of symptoms' is a:
questions.e: Long-term.

questions.q: 'Decrease pain/discomfort in the current session' is a:
questions.e: Short-term.

questions.q: SUDS stands for:
questions.e: Subjective Units of Discomfort Scale.

questions.q: On the SUDS scale, 1 means:
questions.e: 1 = best, 10 = worst.

questions.q: On the SUDS scale, 10 means:
questions.e: 10 = worst.

questions.q: When should you ask the client for a SUDS rating?
questions.e: In red on the slide: before and after each therapy.

questions.q: The SUDS scale runs from:
questions.e: Scale 1 through 10.

questions.q: Where should you review a client's medical history?
questions.a: In a private, quiet area where others can't overhear
w: On the table during the massage
At the front desk with other clients present
questions.e: Confidentiality: private area, before the client undresses. (Location is not on slides.)

questions.q: Reviewing the client's health history is part of the:
questions.e: Bolded on the pre-massage interview slide.

questions.q: The medical history review should happen:
questions.a: Before the massage, while the client is still dressed
questions.e: Pre-massage, clothed and seated.

questions.q: Which is part of the pre-massage interview?
questions.a: Orienting the client to the room
questions.e: Includes greeting, explaining services, reviewing history, consent, orienting to the room.

questions.q: If you make a mistake in SOAP notes, you should:
questions.a: Draw a single line through it, write the correction, and initial and date it
w: Tear out the page and start over
questions.e: SOAP notes are legal records; the original must stay readable. (Not on slides; standard practice.)

questions.q: Why should errors in SOAP notes NOT be erased?
questions.a: SOAP notes are legal documents and the original must stay readable
questions.e: Legal record.

questions.q: Which correction method is acceptable?
questions.a: Single line through the error, initialed and dated
w: Writing over the error in pencil
questions.e: Single line, initial, date.

questions.q: The systolic number is:
questions.a: The top number; where you HEAR the first beat
w: The bottom number; where the pulse disappears
questions.e: Systolic = top, first beat heard.

questions.q: The normal range for systolic blood pressure given in class is:
questions.e: Systolic 80-140; diastolic 50-88.

questions.q: Based on the class range, a systolic reading is considered HIGH above:
questions.e: Normal systolic tops out at 140.

questions.q: Normal blood pressure is considered:
Blood pressure is a good indicator of:
questions.e: Highlighted: a good indicator of overall health.

questions.q: The diastolic number is:
questions.a: The bottom number; where the pulse disappears
w: The top number; where you hear the first beat
questions.e: Diastolic = bottom ('D = Down'), pulse disappears.

questions.q: The normal range for diastolic blood pressure given in class is:
questions.e: Diastolic 50-88.

questions.q: Which BP number is believed to be the more important of the two?
questions.e: Diastolic is believed to be the more important number.

questions.q: Based on the class range, a diastolic reading is considered HIGH above:
questions.e: Normal diastolic tops out at 88.

questions.q: A memory aid for diastolic is:
questions.e: D = Down.

questions.q: The MOST honest form of communication is:
questions.e: Tracking: keep an eye on your client.

questions.q: Tracking is considered the most honest form of communication because:
questions.a: The body reacts involuntarily and shows what the client may not say
w: Clients always tell the truth verbally
questions.e: Wincing, tensing and breath-holding happen without the client deciding to show them.

questions.q: Tracking falls under which type of communication?
questions.e: Non-verbal.

questions.q: Which is an example of tracking?
questions.a: Noticing the client tense up and hold their breath
questions.e: Watching the client's body during the session.

questions.q: The blood pressure cutoff for massage in the student clinic is:
questions.e: In red and highlighted: 170/100.

questions.q: If either BP number reaches the clinic cutoff, you must:
questions.a: Have the CA check, and not do the therapy unless the CA approves
w: Take it again yourself and proceed
Send the client home without telling anyone
questions.e: DO NOT DO THE THERAPY UNLESS APPROVED BY THE CA.

questions.q: A client's BP is 150/100. In the student clinic you should:
questions.a: Get the CA to check before any massage
questions.e: Either number at the cutoff triggers a CA check.

questions.q: When taking BP, the stethoscope is placed over the artery in the:
questions.e: Antecubital area.

questions.q: When taking BP, the cuff is inflated to:
questions.e: 180-200; you should not hear or feel a pulse.

questions.q: With a manual cuff, BP should be recorded as:
questions.e: Even number with a manual cuff.

questions.q: When placing the BP cuff, the bladder goes:
questions.e: Bladder over the artery.

questions.q: Proper fingernail hygiene for a massage therapist is:
questions.a: Short, clean nails scrubbed with a nail brush; no polish or artificial nails
w: Polished nails for a professional look
questions.e: Study guide review answer.

questions.q: Soiled linens should be carried:
questions.e: UP handout: carry soiled linens away from your body; use a plastic-lined linen basket.

questions.q: To prevent cross-contamination of a lubricant, you should:
questions.a: Keep it in a closed container (pump/squeeze) and never dip a used hand in
w: Use an open bowl of oil
Share one jar among all clients
Dip fingers in the jar between strokes
questions.e: Closed containers for lubricants.

questions.q: A lubricant that has been contaminated should be:
questions.e: Study guide review answer: throw it out.

questions.q: Linens used by a client with a parasitic infestation should be:
questions.a: Kept separate, washed in HOT water with bleach, and HOT air dried
questions.e: Treat parasites as 'HOT'.

questions.q: How often should linens be changed?
questions.e: Use clean linens for each therapy.

questions.q: Which glove breaks down when used with oil-based lubricants?
questions.e: Latex breaks down with oil; many people are allergic.

questions.q: Which glove is about 3x more puncture resistant than latex?
questions.e: Nitrile: allergy-safe, high tactile sensitivity, durable, low friction.

questions.q: Vinyl gloves are thicker, which:
w: Makes them break down with oil
questions.e: Thicker = less feel.

questions.q: A client has a latex allergy. Which gloves are appropriate?
questions.e: Both vinyl and nitrile are allergy-safe.

questions.q: Which glove offers high tactile sensitivity and resists oils and chemicals?
questions.e: Nitrile.

questions.q: The best prevention against viruses is:
questions.e: In red and bold on the viruses slide.

questions.q: Any parasitic infestation should be treated as:
questions.a: "HOT": separate sheets, hot water with bleach, hot air dry
questions.e: Bold callout on the parasites slide.

questions.q: Herpes simplex is highly contagious during which stage?
questions.e: At least locally contraindicated.

questions.q: Scabies is caused by:
questions.a: Microscopic mites that burrow under the skin
questions.e: Mites; itchy especially at night, in warm creases.

questions.q: Staph (boils), tuberculosis, strep throat and tetanus are caused by:
questions.e: Bacterial diseases.

questions.q: Protozoa can only survive:
questions.e: Single-celled; cause trichomoniasis, malaria, dysentery.

questions.q: Nits are:
questions.a: White lice eggs that do not fall out easily
questions.e: Head lice eggs.

questions.q: Viruses are hard to treat because they:
questions.e: Easily mutate; difficult to treat.

questions.q: Which is a safety guideline from the lecture?
questions.a: Wipe lubricant from the client's feet
w: Leave oil on the feet for moisture
questions.e: Starred safety guidelines: CPR & first aid, first aid kit, wipe feet, know contraindications, never under the influence.

questions.q: Massage therapists should maintain current certification in:
questions.e: Starred on the safety slide.

questions.q: Therapists must be able to identify:
questions.e: Starred on the safety slide.

questions.q: Which is a sanitation guideline?
w: Massage while ill if wearing gloves
Clean the table once a week
questions.e: Closed containers, clean linens each client, clean table each use.

questions.q: If you are ill, the sanitation guidelines say:
questions.e: Don't massage when ill; avoid massaging ill clients.

questions.q: Who wrote the first book of sports medicine?
questions.e: Highlighted on the Renaissance slide.

questions.q: Galen was the personal physician to:
questions.e: Galen (130-200 AD); his text was used for over 1,000 years.

questions.q: Aulus Celsus, author of De Medicina, is known as the:
questions.e: Bridged the gap between Hippocrates and later times.

questions.q: Ambroise Paré discussed the therapeutic effects of massage especially in:
questions.e: Also classified massage movements.

questions.q: Cherokees and Navajos used massage for:
questions.e: Americas slide.

questions.q: Borelli (Renaissance) is associated with:
questions.e: Borelli 1608-1679.

questions.q: In OH PAIN, the 'N' stands for:
questions.e: Onset, How, Amount, Place, Interaction, Neutralizers.

questions.q: In OH PAIN, 'I' (Interaction) asks:
questions.e: Interaction = worse; Neutralizers = better.

questions.q: Cryotherapy (cold) is used for:
questions.e: Cold = acute; heat = chronic.

questions.q: Thermotherapy (moist heat) is used for:
questions.e: Heat = chronic, hypertonicity.

questions.q: Stretching is defined as:
questions.a: Passively positioning muscle attachments as far apart as possible to elongate the muscle
questions.e: Highlighted definition; increases ROM.

questions.q: Stretching is contraindicated:
questions.e: Highlighted contraindications: disrupts healing, after surgery/fracture, joint inflammation, herniated disc, bone or muscle injury.

questions.q: Which is listed as a relaxation technique to recommend?
questions.e: Highlighted list: deep breathing, meditation, yoga, tai chi, aromatherapy, music/art therapy, biofeedback, hydrotherapy.

questions.q: Which item is part of the intake form?
questions.e: Contact info, health/medical history, major complaint, daily activities.

questions.q: When applying cold packs or ice, you should:
questions.a: Place a barrier between the skin and the cold
w: Rub ice firmly into the skin
questions.e: Barrier between skin and cold.

topics.5: Baseline position for balance and alignment
topics.7: What is used for postural assessment
topics.13: How the client stands for a baseline assessment
topics.28: NYS cautions, local contraindications, clinic rules

questions.q: Gait is defined as:
w: The range of motion of the hip
questions.e: Gait = a person's walking pattern.

questions.q: 'The manner in which a person moves on foot' describes:
questions.e: Handout definition of gait.

questions.q: A client's walking pattern is called their:
questions.e: Gait = walking pattern. (Cadence is steps per minute.)

questions.q: Observing how a client walks from the front, back and side is called:
questions.e: Salvo: ask the client to walk at a normal pace and watch from the front, back and side.

questions.q: Which statement about gait is TRUE?
questions.a: It is a pattern of movement used while walking or running
w: It is the position of the body over a base of support
It is measured with a plumb line only
It never changes with injury or age
questions.e: Gait patterns are influenced by health, disease, injury, age and more.

questions.q: A normal gait should be:
questions.e: The three qualities: smooth, coordinated, rhythmic.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the 3 qualities of a normal gait?
questions.e: Smooth, coordinated, rhythmic.

questions.q: In a normal gait, the arms:
questions.a: Swing forward in opposition to the legs
w: Are held slightly flexed in front of the body
questions.e: Arms extended at the sides, swinging forward in opposition to the legs.

questions.q: During a normal gait, the posture is _____ and the eyes are _____.
questions.e: Posture erect, eyes looking forward.

questions.q: Per the handout, in a normal gait the toes point:
questions.a: Forward, with feet about hip-width apart
questions.e: Toes point forward, feet hip-width apart; thumb and forefinger point forward.

questions.q: Posture is defined as:
questions.a: The position of the body in space
w: The study of anatomy as it relates to work
The curvature of the lumbar spine
questions.e: Posture = position of the body in space (standing, sitting, lying prone, lying supine).

questions.q: The handout defines posture as the position of the body:
questions.e: Posture: the position of the body over a base of support.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the positions of posture listed in the lecture?
questions.e: Standing, sitting, lying prone, lying supine.

questions.q: The slide says posture:
questions.a: Will tell you just about everything
questions.e: Posture 'will tell you just about everything.'

questions.q: Standing posture is maintained by:
questions.a: The strength and tone of muscles against gravity
questions.e: Strength & tone of muscles against gravitational forces.

questions.q: Muscles maintain standing posture by working against:
questions.e: Strength and tone of muscles against gravity.

questions.q: Which two qualities of muscle maintain your posture?
questions.e: Strength & tone of muscles.

questions.q: Muscles that help maintain the body's position are called:
questions.e: Postural muscles maintain position; phasic muscles provide movement.

questions.q: Which position is the baseline measure of balance and alignment?
questions.e: Standing is considered the baseline measure of balance and alignment.

questions.q: Why is standing used as the baseline for posture?
questions.a: Posture there is maintained by muscle strength and tone against gravity
w: It is the most comfortable position
questions.e: Standing = baseline because muscles must hold the body against gravity.

questions.q: To get a baseline measure of a client's balance and alignment, the client should be:
w: Lying face down on the table
questions.e: Standing = baseline.

questions.q: Salvo describes a postural assessment as an evaluation of the client's posture while:
questions.e: Static postural assessment: relaxed, barefoot, standing.

questions.q: When formulating a treatment plan, which should you consider?
questions.a: Health history, the chief complaint and your assessment findings
w: Only what the client prefers to talk about
Only the strokes you like to use
questions.e: Documentation covers history, reason for care, interview and exam findings, and a suggested course of treatment.

questions.q: In SOAP notes, short- and long-term goals and home care go in the:
questions.e: Plan = the day's treatment, short- and long-term goals, and home care.

questions.q: Gait analysis and postural assessment findings are recorded as:
questions.e: Objective = observable, measurable findings, incl. gait analysis & postural assessment, vital signs, ROM.

questions.q: A short-term goal for a treatment plan focuses on:
questions.a: The immediate problem, e.g. decreasing pain this session
questions.e: Short-term = IMMEDIATE problem; long-term = restore normal or enhanced function.

questions.q: A long-term goal focuses on:
w: Decreasing pain in the current session
questions.e: Long-term goals: restore function, eliminate pain if possible, decrease frequency & intensity of symptoms.

questions.q: Documentation lets the treatment plan be:
questions.a: Evaluated and modified as the client progresses
w: Skipped if the client pays cash
questions.e: Documentation allows progress to be evaluated and/or modified as needed.

questions.q: What is used for a postural assessment in the lecture?
questions.e: Plumb line analysis: posterior, lateral and anterior views.

questions.q: A plumb line shows the:
questions.a: Line of gravity, a vertical line through the center of the body to its base
w: Range of motion of each joint
The client's center of mass while walking
questions.e: Salvo: a plumb line determines the line of gravity.

questions.q: Plumb line analysis is done from which views?
questions.e: Three views on slides 5-7.

questions.q: Besides a plumb line, Salvo mentions which tool for postural assessment?
w: A tape measure on the thigh
questions.e: A posture grid gives horizontal and vertical lines as visual cues.

questions.q: The handout's 'Postural Alignment Guidelines' compare a client's posture to:
questions.e: Posture must be assessed and compared to what is considered normal.

questions.q: Which two postural deviations may co-exist?
questions.e: Salvo: 'Hyperkyphosis and hyperlordosis may co-exist.'

questions.q: Rounded shoulders and a dowager's hump are considered mild forms of:
questions.e: Salvo classifies both as mild forms of hyperkyphosis.

questions.q: Hyperlordosis is accompanied by:
questions.e: Hyperlordosis: exaggerated lumbar curve and increased anterior pelvic tilt.

questions.q: An exaggerated thoracic curve often appears together with:
w: A lateral curve of the neck only
questions.e: Kyphosis and lordosis may co-exist.

questions.q: Kyphosis is an excessive curvature of the _____ spine; lordosis is an excessive curvature of the _____ spine.
questions.e: Handout: lordosis = lumbar, kyphosis = thoracic, scoliosis = lateral.

questions.q: Which is TRUE regarding postural muscles?
questions.a: They tend to shorten and strengthen when stressed
w: They tend to lengthen and weaken when stressed
questions.e: Postural muscles shorten and strengthen when stressed (study guide answer).

questions.q: Which pair are examples of postural muscles?
questions.e: Handout examples of postural muscles.

questions.q: Muscles that provide movement, such as the abdominals and gluteus maximus, are called:
questions.e: Phasic muscles provide movement.

questions.q: When stressed, the iliopsoas and erector spinae tend to:
questions.e: These are postural muscles: they shorten and strengthen under stress.

questions.q: Postural muscles mainly:
questions.e: Postural = maintain position; phasic = movement.

questions.q: Common abnormalities in gait result from:
questions.a: Muscle weakness, postural imbalance, pain, connective tissue restrictions
questions.e: Red text on the slide.

questions.q: Which is NOT listed on the slide as a cause of gait abnormalities?
questions.e: Causes: muscle weakness, postural imbalance, pain, CT restrictions.

questions.q: A limp adopted to avoid pain on a weight-bearing structure is called:
questions.e: Salvo: antalgic gait = limp to avoid pain.

questions.q: Per the handout, gait can be adversely affected by:
questions.a: Surgeries that fuse joints and neurologic conditions
questions.e: Also: pain, trauma, muscle imbalance, myofascial restrictions, arthritic changes.

questions.q: Postural imbalance is a cause of:
questions.e: Gait abnormalities result from muscle weakness, postural imbalance, pain, CT restrictions.

questions.q: Post-massage recommendations help to:
questions.a: Preserve and prolong the benefits of a massage
w: Replace the need for future massages
questions.e: Post Massage Recommendations: help preserve and prolong the benefits.

questions.q: Which is a post-massage recommendation from the lecture?
questions.a: Engage in relaxing activities and avoid stress
w: Go straight to a heavy workout
Take a very hot shower to increase inflammation
questions.e: Relaxing activities, cryo/thermotherapy, avoid stress, stretch/exercise, self-massage, referral, follow-up.

questions.q: Referring a client to a PCP or DC is part of:
questions.e: Referral to PCP, DC is on the post-massage recommendations list.

questions.q: The handout recommends a post-massage bath that is:
questions.e: Warm, not cold and not scorching hot (which increases inflammation).

questions.q: Why does the handout suggest eating after a massage?
questions.a: Massage affects circulation and digestion; light-headedness may come from not eating
w: To prevent the client from rescheduling
questions.e: Your body needs to refuel after a massage.

questions.q: Self-massage tools mentioned for clients include:
questions.a: A bouncy ball, golf ball or lacrosse ball
questions.e: Self-massage and prevention measures slide.

questions.q: Structural misalignment is often the source of:
questions.e: Misalignment: structural misalignment is often the source of chronic pain.

questions.q: Misalignment can cause:
questions.a: Degenerative disc disease, chronic myofascial pain and compensation
questions.e: Listed on the misalignment slide.

questions.q: Which is a sign of structural misalignment?
questions.a: Visible deviation from the midsagittal, coronal or horizontal planes
questions.e: Signs: visual deviation from the planes, chronic pain, spasm and trigger points.

questions.q: Which is listed as a CAUSE of structural misalignment?
questions.a: Muscle imbalance between anterior and posterior muscles
questions.e: Also: trauma, aging, emotional stress, obesity, repetitive overuse, leg-length difference, fallen arches.

questions.q: A difference in leg length or fallen arches can cause:
questions.e: Both are on the handout's list of causes.

questions.q: For a baseline postural assessment, the client should be standing:
w: With feet together and arms raised
questions.e: Purple text on every plumb line slide: standing naturally, not in anatomical position.

questions.q: Why should the client NOT stand in anatomical position for a baseline?
questions.a: You want to see their natural posture
w: Anatomical position is uncomfortable for the therapist
questions.e: Baseline = standing naturally.

questions.q: Salvo tells you to have the client stand upright, look straight ahead, relax their shoulders and:
questions.e: Relaxed, barefoot standing posture.

questions.q: Assessing posture with the client in anatomical position is:
questions.a: Incorrect: the client should stand naturally
questions.e: STANDING NATURALLY, not in anatomical position.

questions.q: An endangerment site is:
questions.a: An area with superficial, delicate, relatively unprotected structures that are prone to injury
w: Any area with a lot of muscle
A place where the client feels ticklish
An area that must always be draped
questions.e: Definition from the slide and the 'Quiz material' handout.

questions.q: Why are endangerment sites prone to injury?
questions.a: Their structures are superficial and relatively unprotected
w: They are covered by thick fascia
questions.e: Superficial, delicate structures not well protected by bones and muscles.

questions.q: Over an endangerment site, you should use:
questions.a: Very light pressure or none at all
questions.e: Salvo: only very light pressure, or no pressure, over endangerment sites.

questions.q: Which structures make an area an endangerment site?
questions.a: Nerves, blood vessels, organs, glands, lymph nodes, small bony projections
questions.e: Listed on the slide.

questions.q: Which of these is an endangerment site?
questions.e: Popliteal fossa (back of the knee) is on the handout's list.

questions.q: Which of these is an endangerment site?
questions.e: Anterior triangle: carotid artery, jugular vein, thyroid, trachea.

questions.q: Which of these is an endangerment site?
questions.e: Axilla: axillary artery, brachial plexus, lymph nodes.

questions.q: Which of these is an endangerment site?
questions.e: Femoral triangle: femoral artery, vein and nerve.

questions.q: Which of these is an endangerment site?
questions.a: Kidney area of the low back
questions.e: Kidney area (floating ribs) is a posterior endangerment site.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT on the endangerment sites list?
questions.e: Gluteus maximus is a large muscle, not an endangerment site.

questions.q: The 'upper abdomen' endangerment site is marked by which bony landmark?
questions.e: Upper abdomen (xiphoid process).

questions.q: The cubital area endangerment site is also called the:
questions.e: Cubital area (ulnar notch) at the elbow.

questions.q: The fibrous band down the center of the abdomen that is an endangerment site is the:
questions.e: Linea alba = fibrous band down the center of the abdomen.

questions.q: Just above the clavicle is the:
questions.e: Posterior triangle: brachial plexus, subclavian artery, external jugular.

questions.q: Salvo notes the most serious adverse events have been linked to pressure on the:
questions.e: The most serious AEs are associated with pressure applied to the neck.

questions.q: Another name for endangerment sites is:
questions.e: Endangerment Sites OR Cautionary Sites.

questions.q: 'Cautionary sites' is another name for:
questions.e: Same thing.

questions.q: Salvo also calls endangerment sites:
questions.e: Also called cautionary sites or areas of caution.

questions.q: Salvo's Figure 8-49 is titled:
questions.e: Figure 8-49 Cautionary sites (the calendar's 'Diagram Figure 8-').

questions.q: What are the 2 types of contraindications?
questions.e: Red text: absolute and local contraindications.

questions.q: An absolute contraindication means:
questions.a: You would NOT work on the client at all
w: Massage only with a doctor in the room
questions.e: Absolute: a condition where you would NOT work on them at all.

questions.q: A local contraindication means:
questions.a: Avoid the affected area but massage the rest of the body
questions.e: Local: avoid the affected area; can be done on the rest of the body.

questions.q: In the NYIM clinic, a BP of 170/100 is listed as a(n):
questions.e: High BP = 170/100 in NYIM clinic, under absolute contraindication.

questions.q: Contagious viral or bacterial ailments are a(n):
questions.e: Listed under absolute contraindication.

questions.q: A client with a fresh bruise on one shin can still get a massage elsewhere. The bruise is a(n):
questions.e: Hematomas are local contraindications: avoid the area.

questions.q: How often would an MD order massage for a client with an absolute contraindication?
questions.e: Rare that an MD would order massage, but some exceptions do occur.

questions.q: An indication is:
questions.a: A condition for which massage may help alleviate the symptoms
w: A condition where massage must not be done
questions.e: Indication: condition for which research indicates massage may help.

questions.q: A condition in which massage is beneficial is called a(n):
questions.e: Indication = massage is beneficial.

questions.q: 'Research indicates that massage may help alleviate the symptoms.' This defines:
questions.e: Definition of indication.

questions.q: Which is the opposite of an indication?
questions.e: Indication = beneficial; contraindication = should not be done.

questions.q: Which condition is listed on the slide as an indication for massage?
questions.e: Slide examples: tension headaches, hypertonic muscles, stress.

questions.q: Which is an indication for massage?
questions.e: Hypertonic muscles are on the slide.

questions.q: Which is an indication for massage?
questions.e: Stress is on the slide.

questions.q: Per the Indications handout, which is generally indicated for massage?
questions.e: Insomnia: relaxation massage balances the ANS.

questions.q: Per the Indications handout, which is generally indicated for massage?
questions.e: Massage, stretching and gentle exercise are usually the best treatment.

questions.q: Per the Indications handout, which is generally indicated for massage?
questions.e: Massage relieves the masseter, temporalis and pterygoids.

questions.q: Which type of edema does massage help?
questions.e: Edema due to inactivity is indicated; organ-failure and pitted edema are not.

questions.q: Fatigue, whether mental or physical, is:
questions.e: Mental: relieves stress. Physical: removes metabolic wastes.

questions.q: When dealing with extreme cautions, you should:
questions.a: Do your research and use your BEST judgment
w: Ignore it if the client signs consent
questions.e: Extreme Cautions umbrella slide: do your research and use your BEST judgement.

questions.q: With an extreme caution, the general routine:
questions.a: Requires some type of change to fit the client
w: Is done only on the face
questions.e: Highlighted: special considerations or a change to the routine.

questions.q: THE BIG 3 to be aware of are:
questions.e: Be aware of THE BIG 3: FEVER - ACUTE - INFLAMMATION.

questions.q: The signs of inflammation listed with the Big 3 are:
questions.e: (Redness - Swelling - Heat).

questions.q: If you're not sure massage is appropriate for a condition, you should:
questions.e: Diagnosis is not in our scope; check with the doctor when in doubt.

questions.q: Many conditions are OK to massage in the _____ phase but not the acute phase.
questions.e: Subacute = between acute and chronic; massage generally indicated then, not when acute.

questions.q: Per NYS, you should NOT treat a client when:
questions.a: The therapist or client is in an altered state of awareness from substance use
w: The client has never had a massage
questions.e: Red/highlighted: altered state of awareness.

questions.q: Per NYS, you should NOT treat a client who:
questions.a: Refuses to let you confer with their MD
w: Wants to keep their socks on
questions.e: NO consent for consult = do not treat.

questions.q: Which TWO situations does NYS say you should NOT treat?
questions.a: Altered state of awareness, and no consent to confer with the MD
questions.e: Both on the NYS contraindications slide.

questions.q: If the THERAPIST is in an altered state from substance use, NYS says:
w: Treat only if the client agrees
Have the client sign a waiver
questions.e: Applies to the therapist OR the client.

questions.q: A contraindication is a condition in which massage:
questions.a: May NOT be done: it is inappropriate, unadvised or may be harmful
questions.e: Red text: NOT be done; inappropriate, unadvised; may be harmful.

questions.q: Which word best matches 'contraindication'?
questions.e: Inappropriate, unadvised, may be harmful.

questions.q: 'Conditions which massage may be harmful' defines:
questions.e: Contraindication definition.

questions.q: Contraindications are divided into:
questions.e: Two types on the same slide.

questions.q: An extreme caution is:
questions.a: A condition requiring special considerations or a change in the routine
w: A condition where massage is never done
An area that must stay draped
questions.e: Highlighted definition.

questions.q: With an extreme caution, you:
questions.a: May or may not do the massage
questions.e: A circumstance where you may or may not do the massage.

questions.q: Why is a condition labeled an extreme caution rather than a contraindication?
questions.a: Massage may be beneficial, but it needs to be modified
questions.e: Where it may be beneficial but it needs to be modified.

questions.q: Why is phlebitis / DVT a serious caution?
questions.a: Massage could dislodge a clot to the lungs, heart or brain
questions.e: Danger: dislodging the clot (pulmonary embolism, coronary thrombosis, stroke).

questions.q: Why is edema from heart or kidney failure a caution?
questions.a: Circulation may not handle the extra load from massage
questions.e: Back-pressure: the client can't handle increased flow. Pitted edema is always contraindicated.

questions.q: Match: 'A condition in which massage is beneficial.'
questions.e: Indication.

questions.q: Match: 'Avoid the affected area; massage the rest of the body.'
questions.e: Local contraindication.

questions.q: Match: 'Do not work on the client at all.'
questions.e: Absolute contraindication.

questions.q: Match: 'Massage may help, but the routine must be modified.'
questions.e: Extreme caution.

questions.q: Match: 'Superficial, delicate, unprotected structures prone to injury.'
questions.e: Endangerment (cautionary) site.

questions.q: Match: 'Inappropriate, unadvised or potentially harmful.'
questions.e: Contraindication.

questions.q: Match: 'Occurs as a result of pressure or range of motion.'
questions.e: Mechanical response.

questions.q: Match: 'Nerves are stimulated, which in turn activate a reflex arc.'
questions.e: Reflex response.

questions.q: In the posterior plumb line view, the fixed point is the:
w: Slightly anterior to the lateral malleolus
questions.e: Posterior and anterior views: middle of medial malleoli = fixed point.

questions.q: In the lateral plumb line view, the line passes through the:
questions.a: External auditory meatus, shoulder joint and greater trochanter
w: Nasal septum, umbilicus and pubic symphysis
questions.e: Lateral: slightly anterior to lateral malleolus, slightly anterior to knee midline, greater trochanter, trunk midline, shoulder joint, EAM.

questions.q: The fixed point of the lateral plumb line view is:
questions.a: Slightly anterior to the lateral malleolus
w: The middle of the medial malleoli
questions.e: Lateral view fixed point.

questions.q: Which landmark is on the ANTERIOR plumb line?
questions.e: Anterior: medial malleoli, knees, pubic symphysis, umbilicus, manubrium, nasal septum.

questions.q: The top landmark of the posterior plumb line is the:
questions.e: Posterior: medial malleoli, knees, gluteal cleft, spine, EOP.

questions.q: The inferior angle of the scapula should be level with:
questions.e: Other things to look at: inferior angle of scapula level with T-7.

questions.q: The scapulae should be about how far apart?
questions.e: Scapula 3-4 inches apart.

questions.q: Knock-knees are called _____; bowlegs are called _____.
questions.e: 'Gum' keeps your knees together, 'rum' keeps your knees apart.

questions.q: The gait cycle has two phases. What are their proportions?
questions.e: Stance phase = 60%, swing phase = 40%.

questions.q: How many parts does the stance phase have in the lecture?
questions.e: Heel strike, foot flat, mid-stance, toe off.

questions.q: How many parts does the swing phase have in the lecture?
questions.e: Acceleration, mid-swing, deceleration.

questions.q: At heel strike, the dorsiflexors contract:
questions.e: Heel strike: dorsiflexion, concentric contraction.

questions.q: At foot flat, the dorsiflexors contract:
questions.e: Foot flat: dorsiflexion, eccentric contraction.

questions.q: During deceleration in the swing phase, which muscles contract for control?
questions.e: Deceleration: hamstrings contract for control; ends with heel strike.

questions.q: Toe off involves:
questions.e: Toe off = plantar flexion.

questions.q: Acceleration in the swing phase involves which muscles contracting?
questions.e: Acceleration = quads contract.

questions.q: Lordosis is:
questions.a: An inward curvature of the lumbar or cervical regions
w: An outward curvature of the thoracic region
A sideways curvature of the spine
questions.e: Lordosis: inward curvature of lumbar or cervical regions.

questions.q: Kyphosis is:
questions.a: An outward (convex) curvature of the thoracic and sacral regions
w: An inward curvature of the lumbar region
A sideways curvature of the spine
questions.e: Kyphosis: outward (convex) curvature, thoracic & sacral.

questions.q: Scoliosis is:
questions.a: A sideways curvature of the spine
questions.e: Scoliosis: lateral curvature.

questions.q: Dowager's hump is also called:
questions.a: Neck hump, text hump or hunchback
questions.e: Spine curves excessively forward.

questions.q: Hyperlordosis is also called:
questions.e: Salvo: hyperlordosis = swayback or saddleback.

questions.q: Ergonomics is:
questions.a: The scientific study of individual anatomy and physiology as it relates to performing work
questions.e: Highlighted definition.

questions.q: Ergonomics asks how you set up your equipment to:
questions.e: How do you set up your equipment to SUPPORT your body.

questions.q: Per NYS, which is a LOCAL contraindication (massage OK, avoid the area)?
questions.e: Red list: fractures, open wounds, hematomas, varicosities, new scars, burns, foreign bodies/hardware.

questions.q: During the 1st trimester of pregnancy, NYS guidelines say:
questions.e: Pregnancy - 1st trimester - no sacral or abdominal work.

questions.q: Per NYS, you should confer with the client's MD for:
questions.a: Cancer, tumors, and acute or chronic infection
questions.e: Confer with MD: cancer, tumors, acute/chronic infection.

questions.q: Which is on NYS's 'use caution in treating' list?
questions.a: Medication that weakens connective tissue or increases bleeding
questions.e: Also: fever, contagious disease, organ-failure edema, decreased sensation, acute inflammation, phlebitis/DVT, recent surgery.

questions.q: Which is NOT a NYIM clinic-specific contraindication (as of 7-22-24)?
w: Any active infection, even on antibiotics
Treated for osteoporosis in the last 2 months
questions.e: Clinic list: active cancer/chemo, active infection, COVID positive or exposed within 5 days, osteoporosis treatment in last 2 months.

questions.q: A clinic client exposed to COVID 3 days before their appointment:
questions.a: Cannot be massaged in the clinic
questions.e: COVID positive or exposed up to 5 days prior = clinic contraindication.

questions.q: A clinic client with an active infection who is taking antibiotics:
questions.a: Cannot be massaged in the clinic
w: Can be massaged once they start antibiotics
Can be massaged with lighter pressure
Can be massaged on the back only
questions.e: Any active infection, even if taking antibiotics.

questions.q: Edema due to organ failure that is 'pitted' falls under:
questions.e: Edema due to organ failure (CHF, kidney failure) (pitted).

questions.q: A mechanical response to massage occurs as a result of:
questions.e: Mechanical: result of pressure or ROM.

questions.q: Which is a MECHANICAL response to massage?
questions.e: Mechanical: increased circulation, reduced swelling, reduced scar tissue.

questions.q: Which is a REFLEX response to massage?
questions.a: Decreased arousal of the sympathetic nervous system
questions.e: Reflex: decreased sympathetic arousal, relaxation, stretch receptors, vasodilation, reduced BP.

questions.q: A reflex response happens when:
questions.a: Nerves are stimulated and activate a reflex arc
questions.e: Reflex definition.

questions.q: Triggering the muscle spindles (stretch receptors) is a:
questions.e: Listed under reflex.

questions.q: Body mechanics is:
questions.a: Proper use of postural techniques to deliver massage with the most efficiency and least trauma to the therapist
w: The study of the client's gait
questions.e: Definition on the Body Mechanics slide.

questions.q: The Bow / Archer / Lunge stance is used for:
questions.a: Long strokes, down and away from the therapist
questions.e: Bow-Archer-Lunge = long strokes.

questions.q: The Horse / Warrior stance is used for:
w: Long strokes away from the therapist
questions.e: Horse-Warrior = short strokes, multidirectional.

questions.q: Repetitive motion injuries are:
questions.a: Self-inflicted injuries from POOR body mechanics
questions.e: Carpal tunnel, tennis elbow, TOS, rotator cuff strain, tendonitis.

questions.q: What is the number 1 reason people leave the massage therapy industry?
questions.e: Repetitive motion injuries: the number 1 reason people leave.

questions.q: Table mechanics includes:
questions.a: Table height, client positioning, bolstering and draping
questions.e: Anything that has to do with equipment and client.

questions.q: Which is an element of proper body mechanics?
questions.e: Also: check table height, warm up, correct stance, vary strokes, breathe, brace digits, stretch, lift with legs.

questions.q: Per the Body Mechanics handout, when do you contract the chi muscle?
questions.a: On the exhale, as you apply pressure
questions.e: Breathe out: contract chi muscle, apply pressure. Breathe in: relax, return stroke.

questions.q: In the lunge stance, weight shifts onto the forward leg up to about:
questions.e: Beyond about 60 percent, balance could be lost.

questions.q: Stand with your feet angled about how many degrees to the table?
questions.e: Feet angled 45 degrees to the table.

questions.q: 'Zero gravity posture' involves:
questions.a: Tucking the chin, flattening the low back and sinking the sacrum slightly
w: Locking the knees and arching the back
questions.e: Optimum line of force with no blocks at the neck or low back.

questions.q: Draping gives:
questions.a: Therapist professionalism, client modesty and boundaries
questions.e: Draping 'to cover the body with cloth.'

questions.q: The primary comfort consideration in draping is:
questions.e: As the client goes parasympathetic, temperature and BP may drop.

questions.q: Which areas MUST stay draped?
questions.a: Genital region, gluteal cleft and breast area
questions.e: MUST stay draped. In clinic, breasts of both men and women stay draped.

questions.q: Which draping method MUST be used at NYIM?
questions.e: Underlined on the slide: DIAPER DRAPING must be used at NYIM.

questions.q: Local laws on draping are:
questions.a: The minimum standard; you CANNOT use less
questions.e: Follow local laws: the minimum draping standard.

questions.q: If you accidentally expose a client, you should:
questions.a: Look away, re-drape and stay composed
w: Apologize at length and stop the massage
questions.e: If you expose: look away, re-drape, stay composed.

questions.q: When turning a client at NYIM, the client turns:
questions.e: Have client turn toward you (NYIM).

questions.q: When turning a client, you anchor the sheet with your:
questions.e: Anchor sheet with your thighs, elevate sheet on the opposite side at shoulder and hip.

questions.q: Turning supine to prone, after the turn you:
questions.a: Have the client move up into the face cradle and place a bolster under the ankles
w: Have the client move down out of the face cradle
Place a bolster under the knees
questions.e: Prone: face cradle + bolster under ankles. Prone to supine: move down out of the cradle first.

questions.q: Cryotherapy (cold) is used for:
questions.e: Cold = acute; heat = chronic.

questions.q: Thermotherapy should be applied as:
questions.e: Red text: MOIST HEAT (hydrocollator, hot towel cabi, rice packs, sauna, hot tub, bath or shower).

questions.q: Thermotherapy (heat) is used for:
questions.e: Red text: heat for chronic and hypertonicity.

questions.q: Stretching is contraindicated:
questions.a: After surgery or a fracture, or with joint inflammation or a herniated disc
questions.e: Highlighted: when it disrupts healing.

questions.q: Which is a relaxation technique to recommend to a client?
w: A cold plunge right after massage
questions.e: Highlighted list: deep breathing, meditation, yoga, tai chi, aromatherapy, music/art, biofeedback, hydrotherapy.

questions.q: The handout says stretching after massage helps by:
questions.a: Realigning muscle fibers and improving muscle recovery
questions.e: Stretching realigns fibers and trains the nervous system for flexibility.

questions.q: Self-massage between sessions helps the client:
questions.a: Prolong and extend the massage benefits
questions.e: How can the client prolong, extend massage benefits between sessions.

quizzes.blurb: Body mechanics, foot stances, table mechanics, tools of the trade, draping and the draping policy, stroke elements, Swedish guidelines and session timing, effleurage.
quizzes.sgNote: 1–10 are the "MA1-5" study guide (Body Mechanics, Tools, Draping), 11–20 are the "MA1-6" study guide (Stroke Elements, Draping Review). Slides cited are decks MA1-4 and MA1-5.

topics.1: Define body mechanics and why it matters
topics.6: 5 things you need to do your job
topics.12: #1 reason people leave the industry, and why
topics.26: Sheet draping, turning and assisting on/off the table
