questions.q: Body mechanics is defined as:
questions.a: The proper use of postural techniques to deliver massage with the utmost efficiency and least trauma to the therapist
w: The study of how a client walks
The arrangement of strokes in a routine
Adjusting the table for the client's comfort only
questions.e: Definition on the first Body Mechanics slide.

questions.q: Why are good body mechanics important?
questions.a: They let you work efficiently and reduce the risk of injury to the therapist
w: They make the client fall asleep faster
They replace the need for draping
They let you skip the intake
questions.e: Efficiency plus least trauma to the therapist; the notes add that they reduce repetitive strain injuries.

questions.q: Good body mechanics reduce which type of injury?
questions.e: Notes: 2. Reduces repetitive strain injuries (RSIs).

questions.q: Body mechanics is also called:
questions.e: Notes heading: Body Mechanics (Biomechanics).

questions.q: Per the notes, Western culture's approach to body mechanics focuses on:
questions.e: Western = strength and stamina; Eastern = balance and being grounded, which translates into strength and stamina.

questions.q: Per the notes, Eastern culture's approach to body mechanics focuses on:
questions.e: Eastern focus on balance and being grounded translates into strength and stamina.

questions.q: Which TWO things does the notes handout say are needed for proper body mechanics?
questions.a: Proper foot placement and weight distribution
questions.e: Notes point 5: proper foot placement and weight distribution needed.

questions.q: Which is one of the factors involved in maintaining proper body mechanics?
questions.e: Factors: table mechanics, foot stance, leverage, body posture, strength, stamina, breathing, stability, groundedness/centering, balance & flexibility.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the listed components of body mechanics?
questions.e: Draping is part of table mechanics, but 'draping policy' is not on the body mechanics factor list.

questions.q: Table mechanics, foot stance, leverage and body posture are all:
questions.a: Factors involved in proper body mechanics
questions.e: The body mechanics slide lists these as factors.

questions.q: Which list contains ONLY components of body mechanics?
questions.e: Intention/touch/excursion are stroke elements; the last list is the stroke sequence.

questions.q: Balance & flexibility and groundedness/centering are both:
questions.e: Both are on the body mechanics factor list.

questions.q: How many factors does the MA1-4 Body Mechanics slide list?
questions.e: Table mechanics, foot stance, leverage, body posture, strength, stamina, breathing, stability, groundedness/centering, balance & flexibility.

questions.q: The Bow / Archer / Lunge stance is used for:
questions.a: Long strokes, down and away from the therapist
w: Sitting at the head of the table
questions.e: Bow-Archer-Lunge = long strokes, down and away.

questions.q: The Horse / Warrior stance is used for:
w: Long strokes down the length of the leg
questions.e: Horse-Warrior = short, multidirectional strokes.

questions.q: In the bow (lunge) stance, the lead foot:
questions.a: Points in the direction of the stroke
w: Is parallel to the trail foot
questions.e: Lead foot points in the direction of the stroke; trail foot points off to the side.

questions.q: In the bow stance, weight moves:
questions.a: From the trail foot to the lead foot on the stroke, and back on the return
w: Evenly on both feet with no shift
Onto the toes of both feet
questions.e: Weight transfers from trail foot to lead foot when performing the stroke, back to trail foot on the return.

questions.q: In the warrior (horse) stance:
questions.a: Feet are wider than the hips and the toes point forward
w: One foot is far behind the other
The trail foot points off to the side
questions.e: Warrior: feet wider than hips, toes forward; used for short-distance strokes like petrissage and friction.

questions.q: Which stance is best for petrissage and friction?
questions.e: Short-distance strokes such as petrissage and friction use warrior stance.

questions.q: Which stance is used for covering larger areas or when using effleurage?
questions.e: Bow stance: covering larger areas or effleurage.

questions.q: Table mechanics is:
questions.a: Anything that has to do with equipment and client
questions.e: Bold on the slide: anything that has to do with equipment & client.

questions.q: Which list is table mechanics?
questions.a: Table height, client positioning, bolstering, draping
questions.e: Table mechanics involves table height, client positioning, bolstering and draping.

questions.q: Bolstering falls under:
questions.e: Table height, client positioning, bolstering and draping.

questions.q: Table height is part of:
questions.e: Table mechanics = equipment & client.

questions.q: Which is NOT part of table mechanics?
questions.e: Rhythm is a stroke element.

questions.q: Draping is listed as part of:
questions.e: Table mechanics: table height, client positioning, bolstering, draping.

questions.q: Which is one of the principles of body mechanics?
questions.e: Principles: strength & stamina, breath, stability, balance & flexibility, groundedness & centeredness.

questions.q: Per the slide, breath:
questions.a: Paces you, fuels you, centers you and connects you with the client
w: Should be held during deep strokes
questions.e: Breath: paces you, fuels, centers you, connects you w/client.

questions.q: Groundedness & centeredness:
questions.a: Stop you from giving your energy away
w: Increase the speed of your strokes
questions.e: Groundedness & centeredness: stops from giving your energy away.

questions.q: Balance & flexibility is the ability of muscle and nerve to:
questions.a: Take you from a stable static position to a dynamic one and back
w: Lift a client off the table
Keep the sheet in contact with the client
questions.e: Slide definition of balance & flexibility.

questions.q: Per the notes, lack of strength results in:
questions.a: Early fatigue and increased risk of injury
questions.e: Lack of strength = early fatigue, more risk of injury, harder to assist physically challenged clients.

questions.q: Per the notes, stamina (endurance) is improved with:
questions.a: Cardiovascular training about 3 times a week
questions.e: Stamina: enough for all your clients in a day; improve with CV training 3x a week.

questions.q: The notes compare stability to:
questions.a: A pogo stick vs. a tripod
questions.e: Need a stable base to work from: compare a pogo stick and a tripod.

questions.q: Per the notes, balance is the:
questions.e: Balance: ability to work against gravity.

questions.q: Which is one of the things you need to do your job?
questions.e: What do you need to do your job: massage table, face cradle/bolsters/pillows, stool, oils/lotions/creams, linens, music & lighting, storage etc.

questions.q: Which list is ALL tools of the trade?
questions.a: Face cradle, bolsters, linens, massage oil, stool
w: Gait belt, cane, walker, crutches, brace
questions.e: Tools of the trade slide.

questions.q: Linens should be twin sheets, blankets and towels in quantities:
questions.e: Linens: enough to change between clients.

questions.q: Music and lighting are listed as tools for:
questions.e: Music & lighting (ambiance).

questions.q: The stool on the tools list is for:
w: The client to step up on
questions.e: Stool: for you to sit on (sit when appropriate is also an element of proper body mechanics).

questions.q: Besides buying linens, the tools slide asks you to plan:
questions.a: How you will wash your linens, towels and blankets
w: Which client gets the newest sheets
questions.e: How are you going to wash your linens, towels, blankets.

questions.q: Which item is on the 'what do you need to do your job' list?
questions.e: Oils, lotions & creams.

questions.q: Draping is defined as:
questions.a: To cover the body with cloth
w: To wrap a joint for support
To position the client with bolsters
To change the sheets between clients
questions.e: Draping: 'To cover the body with cloth.'

questions.q: 'To cover the body with cloth' is the definition of:
questions.e: Draping definition.

questions.q: Which are the 2 types of draping?
questions.e: 2 types of draping: sheet and towel.

questions.q: The NYIM Draping Policy defines draping as being:
questions.e: Policy item 1: draped (covered) with sheets at all times.

questions.q: Draping covers the client's body with cloth so that:
questions.a: Only the area being massaged is exposed
w: The whole body is exposed for assessment
The therapist can work through the sheet only
questions.e: Expose only the area being massaged.

questions.q: Draping gives:
questions.a: Therapist professionalism, client modesty and boundaries
questions.e: Draping gives: therapist professionalism, client's modesty, boundaries.

questions.q: Why drape? (3 reasons on the slide)
questions.a: Maintains privacy, offers warmth, establishes a boundary
w: Saves oil, keeps sheets clean, speeds the session
Hides posture, prevents gait problems, lowers BP
questions.e: Why DRAPE: privacy, warmth, boundary between client and therapist.

questions.q: Draping establishes a boundary between:
w: The front and back of the body
questions.e: Establishes a boundary between the client & therapist.

questions.q: For the therapist, draping provides:
questions.e: Therapist professionalism; client modesty.

questions.q: For the client, draping provides:
questions.e: Clients modesty.

questions.q: Which is NOT a reason to drape?
questions.a: To let the therapist work faster
questions.e: Privacy, warmth, boundary.

questions.q: The primary comfort consideration when draping is:
questions.e: Primary comfort consideration is warmth.

questions.q: Why does warmth matter more as the session goes on?
questions.a: The relaxed client shifts to a parasympathetic state, and body temperature and BP may drop
w: The client becomes sympathetic and starts sweating
questions.e: As the client relaxes into parasympathetic, body temperature and BP may drop.

questions.q: As a client relaxes during massage, they shift into a:
questions.e: Parasympathetic = rest and digest.

questions.q: When should you check the client's comfort with warmth?
questions.e: Check with the client before & during the therapy for comfort.

questions.q: Warmth provides the client with:
questions.e: Warmth is the primary comfort consideration.

questions.q: In a parasympathetic state, which may drop?
questions.e: Body temperature & blood pressure may drop.

questions.q: Local laws regarding draping are:
questions.a: The minimum draping standard; you CANNOT use less
questions.e: Bold: you CANNOT use less than local law.

questions.q: Which is a rule of draping?
questions.a: Don't lift, fluff or move sheets away from the client
w: Lift the sheet high to check the client
Fluff the sheet to warm it
Remove the sheet for back work
questions.e: Bold on the slide: don't lift, fluff, or move sheets away from the client.

questions.q: If you accidentally expose a client:
w: Stop the massage and apologize at length
Pretend it didn't happen and keep going
Ask the client to fix the sheet
questions.e: If you expose: look away, re-drape, STAY COMPOSED.

questions.q: Which rule is about the sheet itself?
questions.a: Keep the sheet in contact with the client
w: Keep the sheet tucked under the table
Hold the sheet above the client
Use a different sheet for each body part
questions.e: Keep the sheet in contact with the client.

questions.q: Whose comfort and requests do the draping rules say to honor?
questions.a: The client's requests and the therapist's comfort level
questions.e: Honor client's request; respect therapist's comfort level.

questions.q: Which part of the body is exposed during massage?
questions.e: Expose only the area being massaged.

questions.q: Which is NOT a rule of draping?
questions.a: Use less draping than local law if the client asks
w: Expose only the area being massaged
Keep the sheet in contact with the client
questions.e: Local law is the minimum; you cannot use less.

questions.q: The elements of strokes are:
questions.a: The blend of body mechanics, intention, touch, pressure, depth, direction, excursion, speed, rhythm, continuity, duration, sequence and routine
w: Effleurage, petrissage, friction, tapotement and vibration
Table height, positioning, bolstering and draping
questions.e: Giving a massage is more than rubbing skin; it is a blend of these elements.

questions.q: Which is a stroke element?
questions.e: Effleurage is a stroke in the sequence, not an element.

questions.q: Per the slides, giving a massage is:
questions.a: More than just putting your hands on someone and rubbing their skin
questions.e: Opening line of Elements of Strokes.

questions.q: Which list contains ONLY stroke elements?
questions.e: Stroke elements list.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the elements of strokes?
questions.e: Bolstering is table mechanics.

questions.q: The notes say massage is:
questions.a: An art and a science, and application of the elements varies session to session
w: Purely a science with fixed elements
Purely an art with no rules
questions.e: Elements of a Stroke: massage is an art and a science.

questions.q: Which element is listed FIRST in the blend?
questions.e: The list begins with body mechanics and ends with routine.

questions.q: What is the number 1 reason people leave the massage therapy industry?
questions.e: Repetitive motion injuries: the number 1 reason people leave the industry.

questions.q: Why do repetitive motion injuries happen?
questions.a: They are self-inflicted from POOR body mechanics
w: They come from using too much oil
questions.e: Self-inflicted injuries related to POOR body mechanics.

questions.q: Repetitive strain injuries are described as:
questions.a: Overuse injuries that are cumulative in nature
questions.e: Notes: overuse injuries, cumulative in nature.

questions.q: Which is a repetitive motion injury listed on the slide?
questions.e: Carpal tunnel, tennis elbow, thoracic outlet syndrome, rotator cuff strain, tendonitis.

questions.q: Which is NOT listed as a repetitive motion injury?
questions.e: List: carpal tunnel, tennis elbow, TOS, rotator cuff strain, tendonitis.

questions.q: The best way to stay in the field long-term is to:
w: Work faster to see more clients
questions.e: Poor body mechanics cause the RSIs that drive people out.

questions.q: Which areas MUST always stay draped?
questions.a: Genital region, gluteal cleft and breast area
questions.e: Underlined: MUST stay draped.

questions.q: In the NYIM clinic, the breast area stays draped for:
questions.e: Bold: in clinic breast area of BOTH men & women WILL STAY DRAPED.

questions.q: Which is one of the 3 areas that must always remain covered?
questions.e: Genital region, gluteal cleft, breast area.

questions.q: When draping the abdomen, what is added over the breasts?
w: Nothing; the sheet is folded down
questions.e: Use a towel or pillowcase over the breasts when draping the abdomen.

questions.q: A male client in the NYIM clinic asks to leave his chest uncovered. You:
questions.a: Keep the chest draped; clinic rule covers both men and women
w: Ask the supervisor to uncover it
questions.e: In clinic the breast area of both men and women stays draped.

questions.q: Which area is NOT on the 'must stay draped' list?
questions.e: Only genitals, gluteal cleft and breast area.

questions.q: Intention means:
questions.a: The consciously sought goal or desired end of the massage
w: The force applied to the body
questions.e: Intention: consciously sought GOAL or desired end; what is your PURPOSE.

questions.q: Intention underlies:
questions.a: All components of the massage session
questions.e: Underlies all components of the massage session.

questions.q: Which question captures intention?
questions.e: What is your PURPOSE.

questions.q: Per the notes, intention is based on:
questions.a: A plan of action that meets the wants and needs of the client
w: The time left in the session
questions.e: Intention: based on a plan of action; should meet the wants/needs of the client.

questions.q: Per the notes, all other stroke elements are dependent on:
questions.e: All other elements are dependent on intention.

questions.q: 'Consciously sought goal or desired end' describes:
questions.e: Intention definition.

questions.q: Massage movements should move:
questions.e: Direction: centripetal, toward the center/heart.

questions.q: Centripetal strokes follow the direction of:
w: Arterial flow away from the heart
questions.e: In the direction of venous & lymphatic circulation.

questions.q: On the arm, a centripetal stroke moves from:
w: Side to side across the forearm
The elbow outward in both directions
questions.e: Toward the heart = distal to proximal on a limb.

questions.q: 'Centripetal' means:
questions.e: Centripetal = toward the center/heart.

questions.q: Per the notes, effleurage on the extremities is applied:
questions.e: Effleurage is applied on the extremities centripetally.

questions.q: Why do strokes move toward the heart?
questions.a: To follow venous and lymphatic flow
w: To push blood into the fingers
To keep the sheet in place
questions.e: Direction of venous & lymphatic circulation.

questions.q: Which stroke element is related to stance, foot placement and the length of the stroke?
questions.e: Excursion: length of the massage stroke; related to stance & foot placement.

questions.q: Excursion is:
questions.a: The length of the massage stroke, the distance traveled
w: The time spent on an area
questions.e: Length of the massage stroke / distance traveled.

questions.q: Excursion is dependent on:
questions.e: Notes: excursion is dependent on proper foot placement.

questions.q: A long stroke from ankle to hip has a large:
questions.e: Excursion = distance covered.

questions.q: Which stance gives you a long excursion?
questions.e: Bow = long strokes; excursion is tied to stance.

questions.q: 'Distance covered with a massage stroke' defines:
questions.e: Depth is distance INTO the tissue; excursion is distance ALONG the body.

questions.q: Continuity is:
questions.a: The uninterrupted flow of strokes and unbroken transitions between them
w: The repetition or regularity of strokes
The time spent on an area
questions.e: Continuity: uninterrupted flow, unbroken transitions.

questions.q: To keep continuity as you flow around the body, you:
w: Lift your hands between each body part
questions.e: Flow around the body: KEEPING CONTACT.

questions.q: Rhythm vs. continuity:
questions.a: Rhythm = regularity of strokes; continuity = unbroken transitions between strokes
w: Rhythm = order of strokes; continuity = length of strokes
questions.e: Notes: rhythm is repetition/regularity; continuity is the unbroken transition from one stroke to another.

questions.q: 'Uninterrupted flow' describes:
questions.e: Continuity definition.

questions.q: Taking your hands off the client between strokes breaks:
questions.e: Continuity means keeping contact.

questions.q: Overlapping your strokes over joints to connect one body part to the next supports:
questions.e: Swedish guideline 5: connect body parts by overlapping strokes over joints.

questions.q: Sequence refers to:
questions.a: The order of the massage strokes
questions.e: Sequence: order of the massage strokes.

questions.q: The stroke sequence on the slide is:
questions.a: Effleurage, petrissage, friction, tapotement, vibration, ancillary movements
questions.e: Strokes in order: effleurage, petrissage, friction, tapotement, vibration, ancillary.

questions.q: Which stroke usually goes first?
questions.e: Notes: effleurage usually goes first, then petrissage.

questions.q: Which stroke comes right after effleurage?
questions.e: Effleurage, then petrissage.

questions.q: Which comes LAST in the stroke sequence?
questions.e: Sequence ends with vibration, then ancillary movements.

questions.q: 'The arrangement of massage strokes' is:
questions.e: Notes: sequence = arrangement of massage strokes.

questions.q: Where does your pressure come from?
questions.a: Your own body weight, leaning in from the hara
questions.e: Use your own body weight. Lean in: pressure from the hara.

questions.q: To get depth, the slide says to:
questions.a: Lean in and use your own body weight
w: Lock your elbows and push with your arms
questions.e: Use your own body weight; lean in.

questions.q: The hara (dan-tien) is the body's:
questions.a: Center of gravity, near L4-L5 in front of the spine
questions.e: Notes: center of gravity called the dan-tien, at L4-L5 anterior to the spine; center of physical and spiritual balance.

questions.q: 'Work from hara' is listed as:
questions.a: An element of proper body mechanics
questions.e: Elements of proper body mechanics include work from hara.

questions.q: Which is the WRONG way to create pressure?
questions.a: Muscling it with your hands and thumbs
w: Shifting weight onto the lead foot
questions.e: Pressure comes from body weight and hara, not hand strength.

questions.q: Per the notes, who ultimately controls depth?
questions.a: The client, by guarding/tensing or relaxing and letting you in
questions.e: Ultimately the client controls depth.

questions.q: What is it called when you put all the elements together?
questions.e: Bold: Routine = combination of all these ELEMENTS!!!

questions.q: Routine is:
questions.a: The combination of all the stroke elements
w: The time spent on one area
questions.e: Routine: combination of all these elements.

questions.q: Per the notes, routines:
questions.e: Routine: the union of all other elements; routines can change with every massage.

questions.q: Sequence vs. routine:
questions.a: Sequence = order of strokes; routine = all elements combined
w: Routine = order of strokes; sequence = all elements
questions.e: Don't mix these up on the quiz.

questions.q: 'The union of all the other elements' describes:
questions.e: Notes: the routine is the union of all the other elements.

questions.q: Which stroke element is listed LAST?
questions.e: Routine is last because it combines everything.

questions.q: Touch is described as:
questions.a: The medium of the massage; your opening and ending move
w: The force applied to the body
questions.e: Touch: the medium of the massage; to begin & end the session.

questions.q: Pressure is:
questions.a: Force applied to the surface of the body
questions.e: Pressure definition.

questions.q: Depth is:
questions.a: Distance traveled into the body's tissue
questions.e: Depth: distance traveled into the tissue; achieved by level of pressure.

questions.q: The pressure pattern through a session is:
questions.a: Begin light, gradually increase, deeper specific work, gradually decrease
questions.e: Pressure progression on the slide.

questions.q: Depth varies from:
questions.e: Light, medium, deep.

questions.q: Per the notes, it's usually good to begin a session at the:
questions.e: Touch: usually good to begin at the head, feet or back; a physical introduction.

questions.q: Speed is based on:
questions.e: Bold on the slide: based on the purpose.

questions.q: Rapid strokes are:
questions.e: Rapid = stimulating; slow = relaxing.

questions.q: Slow strokes are:
questions.e: Slow = relaxing.

questions.q: Rhythm is:
questions.a: The repetition or regularity of massage movements
questions.e: Rhythm definition.

questions.q: Rhythm is affected by:
w: Table height, sheets, bolsters and music
questions.e: Affected by excursion, speed, pressure, intention/purpose.

questions.q: Per the notes, strokes that are too fast:
questions.a: Can alarm and fatigue the client, and you can't palpate well
questions.e: Too quick can alarm; fast strokes can fatigue; can't palpate if too fast or too slow.

questions.q: Duration is:
questions.a: Length of time spent on an area or the whole massage
questions.e: Duration definition.

questions.q: Per the Basic Timing handout, head, neck and shoulders get:
questions.e: Supine: head, neck & shoulders 10-15 min.

questions.q: Per the Basic Timing handout, the back gets:
questions.e: Prone: back 10-15 min.

questions.q: Arms and hands, legs and feet, and legs and glutes each get:
questions.e: 5 minutes on each side.

questions.q: In the basic timing order, the client starts:
questions.e: Supine: head/neck/shoulders, arms, legs. Turn prone: legs & glutes, back.

questions.q: What decides how much time a body part gets?
questions.a: The discomfort or condition of the muscle tissue; more time on one area means less elsewhere
w: The order on the intake form
questions.e: Handout note under the timing table.

questions.q: General Swedish massage guideline: work from:
questions.a: General to specific, then back to general
w: The feet to the head always
questions.e: Guideline 1.

questions.q: Swedish guideline on pressure: work from:
questions.a: Light stroking to gradually deeper work, then back to lighter
questions.e: Guideline 2.

questions.q: 'Be thorough. Be complete.' means:
w: Spend most time on the back
Use every stroke on every body part
questions.e: Guideline 3.

questions.q: Swedish guidelines say to work with your own:
questions.e: Guideline 4: work with your own weight and breath.

questions.q: How deep should you work, per the guidelines?
questions.a: Deeply enough to contact and release tension
questions.e: Guideline 6.

questions.q: The last Swedish guideline is:
questions.a: Stay with yourself. Stay centered. Stay grounded.
questions.e: Guideline 7.

questions.q: Per the NYIM Draping Policy, students receiving massage are draped:
w: Only when the instructor is present
questions.e: Policy item 1.

questions.q: Walking from the dressing room to the table, the student wraps a sheet:
questions.a: Horizontally around the trunk for minimum exposure
w: Over the shoulders like a cape
Not at all; robes are used
questions.e: Policy item 3.

questions.q: Once the client is on the table, draping responsibility shifts to:
questions.a: The student acting as the therapist
questions.e: Policy item 4.

questions.q: When the massage is over, the student therapist should:
questions.a: Help the client stay fully covered while getting off the table
w: Remove the sheet for the client
Ask the client to fold the sheets
questions.e: Policy item 6.

questions.q: The policy box stresses developing an attitude of:
questions.a: Non-judgment of physical appearance; treat every body the same
questions.e: Box at the bottom of the policy.

questions.q: To prepare, students receiving massage disrobe:
questions.a: In a bathroom or dressing room
questions.e: Policy item 2.

questions.q: Which draping method MUST be used at NYIM?
questions.e: Underlined: DIAPER DRAPING must be used at NYIM.

questions.q: Which sheets are best for draping?
questions.a: Twin size; 2 sheets required (fitted & top, or top & top)
questions.e: Twin size best; 2 sheets required; fold down top sheet.

questions.q: When turning a client at NYIM, the client turns:
questions.e: Have client turn toward you (NYIM).

questions.q: When turning, you anchor the sheet with your:
questions.a: Thighs, and lift the sheet on the opposite side at the shoulder and hip
questions.e: Anchor sheet with your thighs, elevate on the opposite side.

questions.q: First step when turning a client either way:
w: Ask them to move into the face cradle
questions.e: Both directions start by removing positioning equipment.

questions.q: Turning prone to supine, before the turn the client:
questions.a: Moves DOWN out of the face cradle
w: Moves up into the face cradle
Gets a bolster under the ankles
questions.e: Prone to supine: move down out of the face cradle.

questions.q: Assisting a client on/off the table, you:
questions.a: Lift with your legs, keep boundaries, maintain modesty and ensure safety
w: Lift with your back to move quickly
Remove the drape to see their footing
questions.e: Assisting slide.

questions.q: Which is a way to avoid RSIs?
w: Use the same stroke all session
questions.e: Avoid RSIs: vary strokes, stretch, proper table height, space clients, avoid sustained pressure, stay fit, get massages.

questions.q: Which does NOT help prevent RSIs?
questions.e: Avoid sustained pressure.

questions.q: Which is an element of proper body mechanics?
questions.e: Also: check table height, warm up, vary strokes, work from hara, breathe, stretch, sit when appropriate, lift with legs, honor your limits.

questions.q: 'Honor your limits' and 'find your rhythm' are:
questions.e: Elements of proper body mechanics slide.

questions.q: Physical fitness is:
questions.a: The ability to carry out daily tasks with enough energy left to enjoy leisure and meet emergencies
w: Being able to lift the table alone
questions.e: Physical fitness definition.

questions.q: Per the notes, receiving massages regularly helps the therapist:
questions.e: One of the ways to avoid RSIs.

questions.q: Effleurage is a:
questions.e: Effleurage: a gliding stroke, one or two hands.

questions.q: Effleurage is used for:
questions.a: Introducing touch, applying lubricant, and assessing tissue
questions.e: Introducing touch, applying lubricant, assessing and exploring tissues.

questions.q: Light effleurage used to finish a body part or the session is called:
questions.e: Nerve strokes are a light effleurage.

questions.q: Deep effleurage is also called:
questions.e: Deep effleurage = ironing.

questions.q: With effleurage on the extremities, you work:
questions.e: Work proximal then distal on the extremities; strokes go toward the heart.

questions.q: During effleurage, pressure on the return (dragging hands back) is:
questions.a: Less than on the applied stroke
questions.e: Less pressure when dragging hands back.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of effleurage?
questions.e: Benefits: warms tissues, relaxing, soothing, flushes congestion, passive stretch, blood & lymph flow, relieves insomnia.
